section_summary: This section centers on the detention of Japanese naval officer Yoshio Matsuda after he photographed waterfront and naval sites at St. Petersburg, Florida, and on the State Department’s effort to combine an expression of regret with warnings about suspicious Japanese activities. It also documents claims of Japanese propaganda in American schools, cultural outreach, alleged Japanese-German espionage, Japanese fishing-vessel activity, and an anonymous New York spy-ring allegation that investigators found baseless. Later materials concern Japanese-language schools, the naturalization of Japanese World War veterans, and efforts to rebut sensational claims about armed Japanese residents.

subfiles.title: Continuation of memorandum on the Matsuda detention
subfiles.about: The fragment assesses the immigration authorities’ treatment of Yoshio Matsuda and possible diplomatic handling of the incident.
subfiles.summary: Mr. Ward argues that the Department of Labor should present the strongest possible justification for the immigration authorities’ actions, noting that an officer later entertained and housed Matsuda. He also suggests asking the Japanese Embassy to discourage Japanese government officers from taking photographs under suspicious circumstances.

subfiles.title: Conversation with K. Fujii concerning Yoshio Matsuda
subfiles.from: W. T. Turner, Department of State
subfiles.about: K. Fujii informally requests an explanation for Matsuda’s detention and photographing in a Florida jail.
subfiles.summary: Fujii says Matsuda innocently photographed Florida harbors, was detained without identification papers, and was refused an immediate opportunity to contact Japanese representatives. He emphasizes the humiliation caused by newspaper photographs of Matsuda behind bars and requests an explanation without making a formal protest. Turner promises to refer the matter to the appropriate authorities.

subfiles.title: Precedent involving American naval officers detained at Yokohama
subfiles.about: The memorandum records a Japanese detention of American naval officers as a counterexample to Fujii’s claim that American officials had not received similar treatment.
subfiles.summary: Around 1929, Commander Stonestreet and three other American naval officers were locked in Yokohama police cells after lacking enough money for a taxi fare. They were denied contact with the American consul until the next morning, when Turner secured their release and received an informal police apology.

subfiles.title: Routing memorandum on the Matsuda case
subfiles.about: The memorandum forwards recommendations and a proposed oral statement concerning Matsuda.
subfiles.summary: The Division transmits its January 11 assessment of the case and notes that the Japanese Embassy’s inquiry was informal and oral. It recommends inviting the Japanese ambassador to receive an oral statement if the proposed conclusions are approved.

subfiles.title: Memorandum regarding the case of Lieutenant Commander Matsuda
subfiles.about: The memorandum reconstructs Matsuda’s detention and recommends expressing limited regret while criticizing his suspicious conduct.
subfiles.summary: Based on Navy and Labor Department reports, the memorandum details Matsuda’s cameras, photographs of the USS Trenton and waterfront facilities, lack of identification, detention, and release into Inspector Roux’s custody. It considers confinement behind bars and press photography regrettable but finds that Matsuda’s conduct created reasonable suspicion. It recommends pairing an expression of regret with a firm warning about Japanese officers engaging in apparent intelligence-gathering activities.

subfiles.title: Navy letter on Matsuda’s impaired usefulness
subfiles.from: William H. Standley, Chief of Naval Operations
subfiles.about: The Navy concludes that publicity surrounding Matsuda’s activities has impaired his usefulness in his New York assignment.
subfiles.summary: The letter describes Matsuda as attached to the Japanese Naval Inspection Office in New York and as having engaged extensively in activities outside his assigned duties. It states that public knowledge of the case has materially reduced his usefulness in that position.

subfiles.title: Naval Intelligence account of Matsuda’s activities
subfiles.about: The report describes Yamaguchi’s apology and the intelligence implications of Matsuda’s photography during his journey to Florida.
subfiles.summary: Captain Yamaguchi told the Director of Naval Intelligence that he regretted Matsuda’s conduct and was prepared to send him home, citing the earlier Kanamoto case. The report inventories photographs of the USS Trenton, piers, yacht basins, a blimp hangar, and other sites from Richmond to Miami. It adds that Matsuda lacked papers and may initially have misrepresented himself as a reserve officer studying at Columbia University.

subfiles.title: Proposed oral statement on the Matsuda incident
subfiles.about: The proposed statement combines regret for Matsuda’s detention with criticism of his suspicious photography.
subfiles.summary: The draft recites Matsuda’s apprehension, lack of identification, limited time in a police cell, and release after his status was confirmed. It regrets both the detention and the failure to prevent press photography. It nevertheless attributes the incident primarily to Matsuda’s own conduct and notes the naval attaché’s offer to end his assignment.

subfiles.title: William Phillips memorandum of conversation with Ambassador Saito
subfiles.about: Phillips records his warning to Ambassador Saito about Japanese naval officers’ suspicious extracurricular activities.
subfiles.summary: Phillips expressed regret for Matsuda’s detention and photographing but used the meeting to complain about a broader pattern of Japanese naval activity in the United States. Saito said Matsuda acted on his own initiative, had been reprimanded by Tokyo, and would remain in New York only until his assignment expired in May. Phillips believed Saito would try to prevent repetitions.

subfiles.title: Confidential transmittal to Ambassador Grew
subfiles.from: William Phillips, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Phillips sends Grew confidential copies of three memoranda on the Matsuda case.
subfiles.summary: The letter forwards the January 11, January 16, and January 22 memoranda concerning Matsuda’s detention in Florida. The material is supplied strictly for Grew’s confidential information.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of McClatchy propaganda materials
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Hornbeck acknowledges materials alleging Japanese propaganda in American schools.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck confirms receipt of McClatchy’s letter and statements entitled “Japanese Propaganda in American Public Schools” and “Japan’s Psychology and American Interests.” He also acknowledges a Japan Times item on distributing Japanese textbooks in American high schools.

subfiles.title: McClatchy letter to Secretary Hull on Japanese school propaganda
subfiles.about: McClatchy alerts Hull to an alleged Japanese plan to distribute textbooks and national-defense material through American schools.
subfiles.summary: McClatchy claims Japan intends to introduce Japanese-prepared texts into American public schools and distribute defense-policy material through Japanese-language schools. He emphasizes the large Japanese student population in Hawaii and offers supporting documents for inspection.

subfiles.title: Japanese Propaganda in American Public Schools
subfiles.about: The release portrays proposed Japanese educational materials as government-directed propaganda.
subfiles.summary: The statement cites the Sino-Korean Peoples League, Setsuichi Aoki, and Mr. Okada in support of allegations that Japan planned systematic influence in American and Hawaiian schools. It argues that Japanese textbooks, pictorial material, and national-defense instruction would undermine Americanization among Japanese American children.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Psychology and American Interests
subfiles.about: The release connects Japanese imperial ideology with foreign expansion and propaganda in the United States.
subfiles.summary: The polemic invokes Matsuoka and Dr. Ichimura to argue that belief in divine imperial rule shapes Japanese expansionism. It presents the proposed school textbooks as one element of an assertive propaganda strategy and cites opposition from the Sino-Korean Peoples League of Hawaii.

subfiles.title: High School Students in U.S. to Be Given Books with Correct Information on Japan
subfiles.from: Japan Times and Mail, reproduced by the California Joint Immigration Committee
subfiles.about: The item describes plans for Japanese-American committees to prepare instructional books about Japan for American high schools.
subfiles.summary: The Society of International Cultural Relations proposed gathering and provisionally compiling material in Japan before joint American-Japanese review. Mr. Lasker of the Institute of Pacific Relations was to be asked for suggestions, and the books would cover Japanese government, economics, society, and art.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs comment on the Rafu Shimpo
subfiles.about: The note dismisses articles identified by Captain Puleston as unremarkable amid widespread tendentious publicity.
subfiles.summary: The writer observes that a large volume of tendentious publicity was already circulating. On that basis, the particular newspaper articles cited by Puleston were not considered noteworthy.

subfiles.title: Naval Intelligence transmittal of the Rafu Shimpo
subfiles.from: William D. Puleston, Director of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.to: Chief, Far Eastern Division, Department of State
subfiles.about: Puleston forwards a Los Angeles Japanese newspaper containing appeals to American-born Japanese.
subfiles.summary: Puleston describes a trend of Japanese protective advice directed at American-born Japanese. He characterizes the paper’s articles as offering cooperation while asserting Japanese prestige and warning against spy hysteria and suspicious American correspondents.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Captain Puleston
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges receipt of Puleston’s letter and the Rafu Shimpo.
subfiles.summary: The brief reply thanks Puleston for his January 31 letter. It specifically acknowledges the enclosed Japanese newspaper published in Los Angeles.

subfiles.title: McClatchy letter to Hornbeck enclosing releases 407–409
subfiles.about: McClatchy sends three releases about Japanese-prepared textbooks and defense-policy material.
subfiles.summary: McClatchy forwards releases 407, 408, and 409 without additional comment. He calls particular attention to planned distribution of material on Japan’s national-defense policy through Japanese-language schools in Hawaii and the mainland United States.

subfiles.title: Japanese Propaganda in American Public Schools, release 407
subfiles.about: Release 407 alleges a coordinated Japanese effort to influence American students through school materials.
subfiles.summary: The release cites Japanese officials, educational organizations, and the Japan Times and Mail as evidence of a textbook and classroom-material program. It warns that such efforts would promote Japanese nationalism and obstruct the Americanization of Japanese American children.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Psychology and American Interests, release 408
subfiles.about: Release 408 interprets Japanese educational outreach as part of a wider imperial and propagandistic policy.
subfiles.summary: The document argues that Japanese ideology legitimizes expansion, treaty violations, and demands upon other nations. It uses the proposed American-school texts as an example of Japanese confidence in propagandizing abroad and repeats the Hawaiian objections.

subfiles.title: High School Students in U.S. to Be Given Books with Correct Information on Japan, release 409
subfiles.about: Release 409 reproduces a Japan Times report on proposed instructional books about Japan.
subfiles.summary: The report outlines Japanese and joint Japanese-American stages for compiling school texts. It says Mr. Lasker would review the draft and notes that the material would be tailored to American high-school students.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck acknowledgment of releases 407–409
subfiles.about: Hornbeck acknowledges McClatchy’s releases concerning Japanese-prepared textbooks.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck thanks McClatchy for his February 8 letter. He identifies the enclosures as releases 407, 408, and 409 concerning a project to introduce Japanese-prepared texts into American public schools.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Psychology and American Interests, duplicate copy
subfiles.about: This duplicate release attacks Japanese imperial psychology and the proposed introduction of Japanese-prepared school texts.
subfiles.summary: The release links imperial ideology to Japanese territorial and diplomatic behavior. It then argues that textbooks planned for American schools illustrate Japan’s systematic effort to win foreign approval.

subfiles.title: Japan Proposes to Instruct Our Public School Students
subfiles.about: Release 410 consolidates the committee’s allegations about Japanese textbook and language-school programs.
subfiles.summary: The release describes the Society of International Cultural Relations, its government connections, and its proposed texts for American high schools. It cites protests in Hawaii and claims Japanese officials had arranged support from educational, religious, and social leaders. It also objects to distributing national-defense material through Japanese-language schools.

subfiles.title: McKinley High School referral of an educational-film solicitation
subfiles.from: F. C. Daniel, principal, McKinley High School
subfiles.to: Division of Investigation, Department of State
subfiles.about: Daniel forwards a circular that he suspects may be Japanese propaganda.
subfiles.summary: The principal reports receiving the enclosed solicitation that morning. Believing it resembles Japanese propaganda, he asks the Department to consider investigating it.

subfiles.title: Nippon Cinema Educational Society film-tour solicitation
subfiles.about: Yamasaki offers English-language films of Japan as a cultural-understanding program for a ten-dollar guarantee.
subfiles.summary: The circular presents an educational film tour showing Japanese landscapes, seasons, sports, festivals, customs, and industries. Yamasaki says he supplies the projector and operator and describes the undertaking as noncommercial, though he requests ten dollars toward expenses.

subfiles.title: Wiley report of alleged Japanese-German espionage cooperation
subfiles.from: John C. Wiley, Counselor of Embassy, Moscow
subfiles.about: Wiley reports Litvinov’s confidential allegation that Japanese intelligence used German agents in the United States and Panama.
subfiles.summary: Litvinov claimed a reliable source had revealed Japanese-German collusion to obtain information on American naval plans, construction, and the Panama Canal. Wiley could not verify the story and noted that Soviet political motives might shape Litvinov’s account. He also described Soviet press efforts to associate Japan with Germany and requested strict protection of the source.

subfiles.title: Phillips acknowledgment of Wiley’s espionage report
subfiles.about: Phillips acknowledges Wiley’s report and says its substance was discreetly shared with American intelligence services.
subfiles.summary: Phillips characterizes Litvinov’s information as somewhat fantastic and of doubtful reliability. Nevertheless, he states that the substance was conveyed informally to military and naval intelligence with instructions to protect the matter carefully.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Ensenada despatch on Japanese fishing vessels
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to a despatch on proposed California restrictions against Japanese fishing vessels.
subfiles.summary: It identifies Ensenada despatch 948 by Smale in file 811.628/151. The referenced despatch concerns amendments to California’s fish and game code intended to restrict Japanese fishing operations.

subfiles.title: Proposed amendment of the California Fish and Game Code
subfiles.from: W. A. Smale, American consul, Ensenada
subfiles.about: Smale evaluates California bills intended to restrict Japanese fishing vessels and warns that they may harm relations and intelligence monitoring.
subfiles.summary: Smale forwards proposed legislation and correspondence from F. A. Cochran concerning Japanese vessels operating from San Diego and San Pedro. He argues that the bills might drive vessels toward Mexican waters, increase secret contacts, and reduce American authorities’ ability to observe their crews. Although he takes possible intelligence activity seriously, he recommends caution and offers to consult Cochran personally.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to memorandum on Japanese fishermen and fishing boats
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a memorandum containing Japanese Embassy arguments about Japanese fishermen and fishing boats in California.
subfiles.summary: It directs readers to file 811.628/154 and identifies Hornbeck with the originating office. The referenced memorandum is described as presenting Japanese Embassy propaganda on the fishing question.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Benjamin W. Jones letter on an alleged Japanese spy system
subfiles.about: The sheet identifies a protest concerning alleged spy activities by Dr. Ashima Takis and others.
subfiles.summary: It refers researchers to Benjamin W. Jones’s letter in file 811.4016/198. The subject is described as activities in the United States connected with a Japanese spy system.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Frank L. Polk file on Japanese interest in African Americans
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a file alleging Japanese friendship and propaganda work among African Americans.
subfiles.summary: It identifies a letter to Frank L. Polk in file 811.4016/201. The material was supplied by Charles O. Heydt and concerned Japanese propaganda directed toward African Americans.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to investigation of the Pacific Movement Association
subfiles.from: R. C. Bannerman, Chief Special Agent
subfiles.about: The sheet records that a Labor Department investigation found no Japanese influence in the Pacific Movement Association.
subfiles.summary: The referenced memorandum reports no evidence of Japanese intrigue in the association’s Chicago activities. It likewise found no Japanese influence in the organization’s Philadelphia venture.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese Consul Tomokazu Hori’s activities
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a clipping about Consul Tomokazu Hori’s advocacy in California.
subfiles.summary: The referenced Navy letter enclosed a newspaper clipping about Hori’s propaganda activities. It portrayed him as urging tolerance of Japanese expansion while condemning discrimination against American products.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to visas for Japanese aeronautical engineers
subfiles.from: Stephan, American consular post at Nagoya
subfiles.about: The sheet summarizes visas issued to Takeo Yasuba and Shigeru Kamiya to study American aircraft design and manufacture.
subfiles.summary: The engineers represented Aichi Tokei Denki K.K., which manufactured military and commercial aircraft in Nagoya. The note contrasts their access to the United States with the secrecy and military guarding surrounding the company’s Japanese factories.

subfiles.title: Gauss despatch transmitting an anonymous spy-ring allegation
subfiles.from: Clarence E. Gauss, American consul general, Paris
subfiles.about: Gauss forwards an anonymous letter alleging that a Japanese spy ring operated in New York City.
subfiles.summary: The despatch states that the Consulate General received the enclosed letter on July 13. Gauss transmits it without endorsing the allegations and leaves its value for the Department to assess.

subfiles.title: Anonymous allegation against Viola Friedmann and the Zemans
subfiles.about: The letter accuses Viola Friedmann and Antony Zeman and his wife of operating a Japanese spy ring in New York.
subfiles.summary: The anonymous writer identifies two Manhattan addresses and claims Friedmann headed the ring. The letter further alleges that the Zemans were unlawfully present in the United States and had recently received registered instructions from local Japanese contacts.

subfiles.title: Pontiac referral of Kohei Takamura’s information request
subfiles.from: Neil G. Brackstene, Airport Manager, City of Pontiac
subfiles.about: The Pontiac airport manager asks how to handle a Japanese request for operational information and photographs.
subfiles.summary: The manager encloses Takamura’s letter after consulting the Bureau of Air Commerce. He observes that it may be merely a form request but offers to follow any State Department recommendation.

subfiles.title: Kohei Takamura request for operational literature
subfiles.to: City of Pontiac Department of Aeronautics
subfiles.about: Takamura requests business information, plans, photographs, and literature explaining the airport’s operations.
subfiles.summary: The short letter asks for the latest descriptive and operational material. It provides Takamura’s address in Kamimeguro, Tokyo, and requests a reply by return mail.

subfiles.title: State Department reply concerning Takamura’s request
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Hamilton advises that Pontiac may either disregard Takamura’s letter or send readily available descriptive publications.
subfiles.summary: The Department sees no reason to withhold ordinary leaflets or bulletins if the city wishes to respond. It returns Takamura’s original letter and thanks the airport manager for referring the matter.

subfiles.title: Internal memorandum on investigation of Friedmann and the Zemans
subfiles.about: The memorandum says two investigative reports largely dispose of the spy allegations against Friedmann and the Zemans.
subfiles.summary: The attached reports are described as refuting the Japanese-spy label applied to the three New York residents. Mr. Burr nevertheless intends to continue monitoring mail delivered to their addresses.

subfiles.title: Decision not to send draft letter to Justice
subfiles.about: The note concludes that Burr’s report makes a proposed letter to the Justice Department unnecessary.
subfiles.summary: The writer reviews the apparent implications of Burr’s investigation. On that basis, the draft communication to Justice is presumed canceled.

subfiles.title: Initial New York investigation of alleged Japanese spy ring
subfiles.from: Special Agent in Charge, New York Division
subfiles.about: The report finds no immediate evidence connecting Friedmann or the Zemans with Japanese agents.
subfiles.summary: Discreet inquiries confirmed the residents and addresses but found ordinary rooming houses, no observed Japanese visitors, and no recent registered mail. Investigators had not yet determined the Zemans’ immigration status. Surveillance and mail monitoring were to continue in case suspicious activity developed.

subfiles.title: Follow-up investigation of Friedmann and the Zeman family
subfiles.from: Special Agent in Charge, New York Division
subfiles.about: The follow-up finds the spy allegation baseless and suggests that Count Kemeny sent it out of spite.
subfiles.summary: Investigators describe Antony Zeman as a law-abiding Hungarian-born upholsterer and Friedmann as his wife’s sister. They trace a personal conflict involving a volatile acquaintance calling himself Count Kemeny, Edward Hard, or Miller, who later appears to have gone to Paris. Although the report finds no vestige of espionage, mail monitoring is continued.

subfiles.title: Departmental conclusion on the alleged New York spy ring
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department informs Gauss that investigation found no spy activity and attributes the anonymous letter to spite.
subfiles.summary: The letter acknowledges Gauss’s July 19 despatch and encloses an excerpt from the New York special agent’s report. Because no evidence of espionage emerged, the Department concludes that the anonymous accusation was probably malicious.

subfiles.title: McClatchy letter on Japanese-language schools
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Far Eastern Division
subfiles.about: McClatchy discusses Japanese-language schools, Japanese American citizenship, and his committee’s relationship with Nisei leaders.
subfiles.summary: McClatchy argues that state and federal limitations leave potentially harmful Japanese-language schools beyond effective control. He reports discussions with Japanese American Citizens League leaders and suggests replacing separate schools by adding Japanese-language study to public high schools. He presents his committee as a candid unofficial instrument for reducing friction with Japan and encloses documents 417, 421, and 425.

subfiles.title: Public Law 162: Naturalization of certain resident alien World War veterans
subfiles.about: The act authorizes naturalization of otherwise racially ineligible resident alien World War veterans who satisfy specified service and residence conditions.
subfiles.summary: The law waives racial bars for qualifying veterans who served before the Armistice, received honorable discharges, and maintained permanent United States residence. It also validates certain earlier certificates and waives documentary fees and several procedural requirements. Petitions had to be filed before January 1, 1937.

subfiles.title: Congressional Recognition of Japanese Veterans
subfiles.about: Release 421 supports carefully limited naturalization legislation for Japanese World War veterans.
subfiles.summary: The release recounts the earlier invalidation of citizenship granted to Japanese veterans and the drafting of a new bill under Representative Clarence F. Lea. It says Consul General Shuh Tomii, California officials, veterans’ organizations, and members of Congress helped shape or support the measure. The committee insists that recognizing veterans should not weaken the 1924 exclusion law.

subfiles.title: “500,000 Armed Japanese!”
subfiles.from: California Joint Immigration Committee; V. S. McClatchy and James K. Fisk
subfiles.about: Release 417 rejects a sensational claim that half a million armed Japanese lived in the United States.
subfiles.summary: The committee calls the figure impossible in light of the much smaller total Japanese population and praises the law-abiding character of many Japanese Californians and Nisei. It nevertheless identifies alien-land-law violations and the southern California fishing fleet as legitimate regulatory concerns. The release supports naturalization of Japanese World War veterans while maintaining the exclusion policy of 1924.
